paras: The lynching of Peter Vinegar, George Robertson and Isaac King took place at Lawrence, Kansas, early on June 10, 1882, when masked men took the three Black prisoners from the Douglas County jail and hanged them from the Kansas river bridge. The men were charged with robbing and killing David Bausman, an Ohio farmer, and were reported to have confessed at a preliminary examination the day before. The case drew national wire coverage, a protest meeting by Black residents, and condemnation from Kansas papers.

Bausman had come to Lawrence in late May to be near his brothers and was said to have shown a roll of bank bills at a saloon. According to the Emporia News, Peter Vinegar's daughter, known as Sis, led him to an icehouse by the river on the night of June 1, where King and Robertson struck him down with a hammer and club.

Vinegar and his daughter were arrested at once, Robertson was captured at Independence, Missouri, and King was caught near Eudora. At Friday's examination Sis Vinegar, King and Robertson were reported to have confessed; an earlier attempt to lynch the prisoners had been stopped by the jailer.

At about 1 a.m., according to the Lawrence Journal, fifty or more men came to the jail and demanded admittance; other accounts put the number at about a hundred masked men. Sheriff Asher refused and resisted but was compelled to submit, and the party cut through the doors and cells with sledge hammers and cold chisels.

The mob took Vinegar, Robertson and King, and a ballot on whether to take Sis Vinegar as well ended with her being left in the jail. With arms pinioned and ropes around their necks, the three were marched about a square to the iron wagon bridge over the Kansas river, Robertson repeatedly falling to his knees to beg for his life. When King asked to be let down easy, the men behind him answered, 'Did you let Bausman down easy?' and pushed him off.

The wire reported that Vinegar's and Robertson's necks were broken and King's was not; the bodies were cut down at about 7 a.m. and placed in the jail yard. Passengers arriving on the Santa Fe midnight train were held by the mob until the hanging was done, and a crowd that could not get near cheered the lynchers as they returned.

Reports that evening spoke of talk of revenge among Black residents, though most were quoted as saying the punishment was deserved. On June 12 a mass meeting of colored citizens condemned both the murder and the lynching, declaring that the prisoners had been entitled to trial in due course of law.

A Lawrence dispatch of the same day reported that the grand jury had indicted four of the mob and that officers were looking for them; no report of arrests or a trial was found. Sis Vinegar was reported in October 1882 to have been convicted of second-degree murder for her part in Bausman's death.

Most white papers carried the press-association wire under headlines such as 'Negro Murderers Lynched,' treating the men's guilt as settled, and a St. Louis dispatch ran under the heading 'Merited Their Fate.' A Kansas City dispatch printed in New Haven reported regret at the town's disgrace but 'not a word of sympathy' for the dead men.

Kansas papers were more critical: the Emporia News called the lynching 'a high-handed outrage' and repeated a hint that 'some of the best people of Lawrence' were involved. The Colored Patriot, a Kansas paper, wrote that lynching had fixed itself as an institution and that Lawrence had 'opened the ball,' adding that disregard of legal forms wronged the living more than the dead. The Omaha Bee headed its report of the colored citizens' meeting 'A Kansas Town Still Bellowing For Black Blood,' and the Russellville Democrat remarked that Kansas had begun to lynch her negro citizens.

Accounts differ on the mob's size, from fifty in the Lawrence Journal and Wichita Eagle to over a hundred in eastern dispatches, and one wire version put the time at ten o'clock. Kansas City and Lawrence reports placed the lynchers among Bausman's rural neighbors with local help, while the Journal reported an assertion that two-thirds of the party were Black men.

bases: A masked crowd broke into the Douglas County jail at Lawrence, took out three Black prisoners charged with murder and hanged them from the Kansas river bridge (A6, A11, A19).

Three prisoners were taken from the jail over the sheriff's resistance by fifty to over a hundred masked men and hanged as punishment for the murder of David Bausman (A5, A11, A19); the papers treat it as summary punishment outside the courts (A32).
Independent wire, Kansas City, St. Louis and Kansas accounts, including the Lawrence Journal's local report, agree on the jail seizure and triple hanging from the bridge (A4, A7, A11, A19).

accounts.label: Colored citizens' meeting
accounts.gist: Resolutions condemned the murder and the lawlessness and said the prisoners were entitled to trial by law.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the wire under headlines like 'Negro Murderers Lynched' and 'Murderers Lynched', treating guilt as settled.
A St. Louis dispatch headed 'Merited Their Fate' explained the lynching by the confessions and examination testimony.
The Emporia News called it a 'high-handed outrage' and the mob 'midnight madmen'.
The Colored Patriot said lynching had become an institution and Lawrence had 'opened the ball'.
The Omaha Bee headlined 'A Kansas Town Still Bellowing For Black Blood' over reports of the colored meeting and indictments.
